issues.legal_issue: A court complaint is not required for prosecution concerning a forged document when only a copy, and not the forged original, was produced in the proceeding.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that a party to proceedings before an officer had used a forged verified claim.
The original claim was not produced before the officer; only an attested copy was submitted.
The Court assumed, without deciding, that the officer was a court for this purpose.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the officer was a court, no complaint by the officer was required because the forged original was not produced before him.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a court complaint is required when the forged document itself is produced or given in evidence, not when only a copy is produced. The Court applied Sanmukh Singh v. The King, (1949) L.R. 77 I.A. 7, which relied on the practical distinction between an original and a copy; it also referred to Girdharilal v. The Emperor, A.I.R. (1925) Oudh 413.

rule.if: document_offense_prosecution and proceeding_party_accused and only_copy_produced and original_forged_document_not_produced

predicates.document_offense_prosecution: A person is prosecuted for an offense concerning a forged document.
predicates.proceeding_party_accused: The person accused is alleged to have committed the offense as a party to a proceeding before a court.
predicates.only_copy_produced: A copy of the alleged forged document, rather than its original, was produced in the proceeding.
predicates.original_forged_document_not_produced: The alleged forged original was not produced in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party is prosecuted for a document offense connected with a court proceeding and only a copy is produced, the court complaint is not required if the forged original is not produced.

issues.legal_issue: Submitting an attested copy that serves the purpose of a forged original can constitute use of that original as genuine when the accused knowingly and dishonestly causes its submission.
material_facts: An attested copy of a claim that had never been verified or issued was submitted with an application for compensation.
The evidence supported the finding that the accused had the claim and copy prepared and attested and had the application and enclosures submitted on his behalf.
The claim was in the accused’s favour, and the Court inferred that he knew it had not been verified and intended to obtain a benefit to which he was not entitled.
The applicable process allowed an attested copy to be submitted instead of the original.
issues.conclusion: The attested copy’s submission amounted to use of the forged original as genuine, and the conviction for using a forged document was rightly upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, penalises fraudulent or dishonest use as genuine of a document known or believed to be forged; it does not require production of the original. Where an attested copy will serve the original’s purpose, submitting that copy can amount to use of the forged original as genuine. Unlike section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 471 does not require production of the forged original. No earlier case was relied on for this proposition.

rule.if: forged_document_use_prosecution and attested_copy_substitutes_for_original and accused_caused_copy_submission and accused_knew_claim_was_forged and submission_sought_wrongful_gain

predicates.forged_document_use_prosecution: A person is prosecuted for using a document alleged to be forged as genuine.
predicates.attested_copy_substitutes_for_original: An attested copy is accepted for the purpose for which the original document would otherwise be used.
predicates.accused_caused_copy_submission: The accused prepared or procured the copy and caused it to be submitted, personally or through another person.
predicates.accused_knew_claim_was_forged: The accused knew or had reason to believe that the underlying claim document was forged.
predicates.submission_sought_wrongful_gain: The accused submitted the copy to obtain a benefit to which the accused was not entitled.

issues.definition: If an accused who knows or has reason to believe that a document is forged causes a functional attested substitute to be submitted to obtain an unauthorized benefit, use of the forged document as genuine is established.

issues.legal_issue: Submitting a forged claim copy to obtain an unauthorized benefit is conduct beyond mere preparation for attempted cheating.
material_facts: The accused’s application and its enclosures, including the attested copy of the forged claim, were submitted to seek compensation.
The claim was used in an effort to obtain an allotment to which the accused was not entitled.
The Court found that the case had gone beyond preparation because the copy had actually been used by being sent or presented to the officer.
issues.conclusion: The conviction for attempted cheating was rightly upheld because the conduct had gone beyond preparation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 420 read with section 511 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and concluded on these facts that actual submission of the forged claim copy in pursuit of an unauthorized benefit went beyond preparation. No earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.attempted_cheating_conviction_appeal: A criminal appeal challenges a conviction for attempted cheating.
predicates.forged_claim_copy_submitted: The accused caused a copy of a forged claim to be sent or presented to support an application.
predicates.submission_sought_unauthorized_benefit: The application sought a benefit that the accused was not entitled to receive.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an attempted-cheating conviction and the accused caused a forged claim copy to be submitted to obtain an unauthorized benefit, the conviction is upheld.
